title: Trump Uses Rare 'Pocket Rescission' to Cut $1 Billion Congress Already Approved
summary:
President Donald Trump is canceling nearly $1 billion in spending that Congress already approved — and he's doing it with a rarely used power that even some members of his own party say is illegal.

The White House announced the cuts Friday. Most target Health and Human Services programs serving refugees and unaccompanied minors accused of being in the country illegally. The administration argues the money is no longer necessary because illegal border crossings have dropped significantly.

Also on the chopping block: a Department of Education program for migrant students, a Department of Justice office focused on reducing racial tensions, a business development initiative for minority entrepreneurs, housing counseling at HUD, and $70 million for what the White House called "woke" international education programs.

The tool Trump used is called a "pocket rescission" — a maneuver that lets a president propose canceling spending Congress approved. Under federal law, Congress gets 45 days to review such cuts before they take effect. But Trump announced them with only five days left in the fiscal year, and the House is out of session until after the November election. That makes the review nearly impossible.

The Government Accountability Office, an arm of Congress, says the maneuver is illegal. Sen. Susan Collins of Maine — a Republican facing a tough reelection and chair of the Senate Appropriations Committee — condemned the move. "Not only is the delay itself an impoundment that was not reported to Congress, but also it is a usurpation of Congress's appropriations powers," she said. "OMB is an agency of the executive branch. It does not get to decide which programs are worth funding."

Sen. Patty Murray of Washington, the top Democrat on the committee, called it "theft from the American people, plain and simple."

The administration argues the power is legally permissible. Last year, Trump used a pocket rescission for the first time in nearly 50 years, blocking $4.9 billion in foreign aid. The Supreme Court declined to block it, citing the president's authority over foreign affairs. This time, the target is domestic spending — and the battle over who really controls the purse strings is far from over.
why_it_matters: This is a live test of the separation of powers: if a president can cancel spending Congress approved by running out the clock, the legislature's most important check on the executive weakens — affecting every program from refugee services to student aid that today's teenagers will inherit as voters.

background_read: Congress holds the 'power of the purse': under Article I of the U.S. Constitution, only Congress can decide how federal money is raised and spent, which is one of its main checks on the president.

That rule was tested in the 1970s, when President Richard Nixon refused to spend billions of dollars Congress had appropriated. Congress responded with the Impoundment Control Act of 1974, which limits a president's ability to hold back money and created the rescission process — a formal way for a president to ask Congress to cancel spending.

The same law gives Congress 45 days to review a rescission proposal; if Congress does not approve it in that window, the money is supposed to be spent. The Government Accountability Office (Congress's own investigative and auditing agency) reviews these reports and said this maneuver is illegal.

In the 1975 Supreme Court case Train v. City of New York, the justices ruled that a president could not simply refuse to release money Congress had voted for. The federal fiscal year ends on September 30, which is why timing is central here: a proposal sent with only days left can run out the clock while the House is out of session.
The Office of Management and Budget (OMB — the White House office that prepares the president's budget) is the agency at the centre of the dispute, and it argues the power is legally permissible.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — the administration and its supporters
perspectives.description: They argue the president is exercising a lawful tool to cut waste, and that with border crossings down, money tied to those programs is no longer needed. From this view, a president elected to shrink government should be able to cancel spending quickly rather than wait on a slow Congress.

perspectives.perspective: Critical — congressional defenders and the GAO
perspectives.description: The Government Accountability Office and senators from both parties call the timing a way to dodge Congress's 45-day review, which they say makes it an illegal impoundment. Senator Collins calls it a 'usurpation' of Congress's appropriations powers, and Senator Murray calls it 'theft from the American people'.

The 1974 Impoundment Control Act was written specifically after President Nixon tried to withhold funds Congress had voted for, and the Supreme Court rejected that in 1975. The key difference now is that the Supreme Court already declined to block last year's foreign-aid rescission, leaving an open legal question about whether domestic spending is treated the same way.

Because the House is out of session until after the November election and the fiscal year ends within days, the review period seems designed to expire on its own. The real decision may end up in court, and the outcome could set the rule for how much spending power future presidents hold.
